title: FBR IRIS API Integration Guide for Pakistan (2026)
metaDescription: A developer's guide to FBR IRIS API integration in Pakistan: tokens, endpoints, sandbox testing, offline sync, and the mistakes that trigger penalties.
keywords: fbr iris api integration guide pakistan 2026
content:
FBR IRIS API integration is the process of connecting a point-of-sale or ERP system directly to the Federal Board of Revenue's IRIS platform over HTTPS, so every sales invoice is transmitted to FBR in real time and returns a fiscal invoice number and QR code before the customer receives their receipt. It replaces manual data entry with a machine-to-machine link.

For a Tier-1 retailer, that link is not optional. Selling through an unintegrated till exposes the business to penalties under Section 182 of the Sales Tax Act — commonly assessed at PKR 500,000 for failure to integrate, alongside disallowance of a large share of input tax credit and, in repeat cases, sealing of the outlet. The integration itself is a few weeks of engineering. The failure to do it is a permanent line item.

How the IRIS connection actually works

Most people picture the FBR IRIS portal — the web interface where returns are filed. The API is a different surface. Your POS software authenticates with a token issued against your registered sales tax profile, then posts a JSON invoice payload to a fiscal endpoint for each transaction. FBR validates the payload, assigns a fiscal invoice number, and returns it with QR data that must be printed on the receipt.

Three technical realities shape every integration:

  • Tokens expire. The bearer token issued for POS transmission is not permanent. Your client must detect a 401 response, silently re-authenticate, and retry the original invoice — not surface an error to a cashier with a queue of customers.
  • Each till is a separate registration. FBR registers machines, not companies. A five-counter store is five POS IDs, each transmitting under its own identifier. Reusing one ID across terminals is a compliance failure, not a shortcut.
  • The invoice number is FBR's to assign. Your internal sequence is bookkeeping. The fiscal number returned by IRIS is what the customer verifies and what an auditor matches against. Read more on what that number means in our guide to the FBR invoice number.

What you need before writing a line of code

Integrations stall on paperwork far more often than on engineering. Have these in hand first:

  • An active STRN (sales tax registration number) in good standing — see our STRN registration guide.
  • Confirmation of your Tier-1 retailer status, which determines whether integration is mandatory and on what timeline.
  • IRIS portal credentials with POS registration rights, plus the registration completed for each physical machine.
  • A static outbound IP or a documented egress range, since access to fiscal endpoints is commonly restricted.
  • A named person who owns the FBR relationship. Every integration hits at least one question only a helpline or RTO officer can answer.

The integration, step by step

  1. Register the business on IRIS and confirm the sales tax profile is active. A suspended STRN blocks token issuance outright, and no amount of debugging on your side will reveal that as the cause.
  2. Register each POS machine through the IRIS portal and record the POS ID returned for every till. Store these in configuration, not hardcoded in the application.
  3. Request sandbox access and obtain test credentials. Never develop against production — a malformed test invoice posted live becomes a real fiscal record you then have to explain.
  4. Build the invoice payload mapping your line items, tax rates, buyer details, and totals to the required schema. Tax rate precision is where most first attempts fail: rounding your own totals before transmission produces mismatches FBR rejects.
  5. Implement token lifecycle handling — acquire, cache, detect expiry, refresh, retry. Wrap the whole transmission in a retry with backoff so a two-second network blip does not become a failed sale.
  6. Handle the response: persist the fiscal invoice number against your internal order, render the QR code on the receipt, and store the raw response for audit. If you keep only your own record, you cannot prove what FBR received.
  7. Test the failure paths — expired token, network loss, rejected payload, duplicate submission — then move to production, roll out one till first, and reconcile a full day of invoices before enabling the rest.

Sandbox and production are not the same environment

Teams routinely lose a week assuming a clean sandbox run guarantees a clean go-live. It does not.

AspectSandboxProduction
Invoice recordsDisposable test dataPermanent fiscal records, auditable
Validation strictnessOften more forgivingRejects edge cases sandbox accepted
CredentialsTest token, test POS IDsLive token bound to your real STRN
MistakesDelete and retryCorrection requires a credit note trail
Rate behaviourLight, unrepresentative loadThrottling under real transaction volume
DowntimeIrrelevantBlocks checkout unless offline mode exists

Offline sales and the buffer that saves you

The single most consequential design decision is what happens when connectivity drops. A retailer on Karachi's Tariq Road does not stop selling because a fibre line is cut, and a system that blocks the sale is a system staff will bypass.

The correct pattern is a durable local queue. The sale completes, the invoice is written to local storage with a provisional receipt, and a background worker transmits to IRIS the moment the link returns, then reconciles the fiscal number back onto the record. Two details matter: the queue must survive a power cut, so an in-memory buffer is not enough; and it must be monitored, because a queue silently failing for three days is worse than no queue at all. Reconcile transmitted counts against sales counts daily.

A real integration, and what it cost

Consider a mid-sized garments retailer — call it Al-Karim Fabrics, four outlets across Lahore and Faisalabad, eleven tills, roughly 1,400 invoices a day at peak. They ran a desktop POS with no fiscal link and received a compliance notice after a field visit.

Their build took seven weeks. Two were engineering; five were spent on a mismatch between the tax rate applied to a discounted bundle in their own system and the rate FBR's validator expected — a reconciliation problem, not a code problem. Direct cost landed near PKR 850,000 in developer time, plus ongoing maintenance whenever schema or rate rules change. The exposure they avoided, at PKR 500,000 per non-integration finding across multiple outlets plus input tax disallowance, was several times that.

The lesson their team drew: the API was the easy part. The hard part was that their own tax logic had been quietly wrong for years, and integration is what exposed it. If you are weighing build against buy, our breakdown of FBR POS integration cost in Pakistan puts real numbers on both paths.

Mistakes that turn an integration into a penalty

  • Treating transmission as fire-and-forget. If you do not check the response and persist the fiscal number, you will discover months later that a subset of invoices never landed — and the burden of proof is yours.
  • Sharing one POS ID across terminals. It works technically and fails legally. Auditors reconcile per-machine.
  • Printing your own invoice number as the fiscal one. The customer verifies the receipt against FBR records; a number that does not resolve is a red flag on your outlet, not theirs.
  • No monitoring on the queue. Every serious failure we have seen was silent for days before anyone noticed.
  • Assuming the schema is frozen. Rate structures and required fields change by SRO. Budget maintenance, and verify current requirements against FBR notifications rather than a blog post — including this one.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to build an IRIS API integration myself?

No. Most Pakistani retailers use a POS or ERP that already ships an FBR-compliant integration, which shifts schema maintenance, token handling, and offline sync onto the vendor. Building in-house makes sense only if you have unusual workflows, in-house engineering capacity, and a willingness to maintain the connection permanently as FBR rules evolve.

How long does an FBR IRIS API integration take?

For a team with a clean tax data model, two to four weeks including sandbox testing is realistic. In practice most projects run six to eight weeks, because integration surfaces pre-existing problems in how the business calculates tax on discounts, bundles, returns, and exchanges. Budget the reconciliation time, not just the coding time.

What happens if the IRIS API is down during business hours?

You keep selling. A compliant system queues invoices locally, issues a provisional receipt, and transmits once connectivity returns, reconciling the fiscal number afterwards. What you must not do is stop transmitting and never catch up — the obligation to report the sale does not lapse because the connection failed, and unreported invoices are what audits find.

Why does my token keep expiring mid-shift?

Because it is designed to. The token issued for POS transmission has a limited lifetime, and a correct client treats a 401 as a routine event: re-authenticate in the background and retry the invoice without the cashier ever seeing it. If expiry is visible to staff, the token lifecycle has not been implemented properly.

Can one integration cover all my branches?

One codebase can, but registration is per machine. Every till at every outlet needs its own POS registration and transmits under its own POS ID. Multi-branch operations should treat the ID mapping as configuration data with an owner, since a mis-mapped till reports another outlet's sales — an error that is painful to unwind after the fact.

Is the FBR sandbox representative of production?

Only partially. Sandbox validates the shape of your payload but is typically more forgiving than production and does not reflect real load. Plan for a phased go-live: one till, one full day, complete reconciliation against your own sales records, and only then roll out the remaining terminals.

How do customers verify what I transmit?

Through the QR code and fiscal invoice number on the receipt, which resolve against FBR's records. Our guide on how to verify an FBR invoice in Pakistan walks through the customer-side flow — worth understanding, because it is exactly what an inspector will do at your counter.

Where to go from here

An FBR IRIS API integration is a modest engineering task wrapped around a demanding data problem. The endpoints are learnable in a day; getting your tax logic, per-machine registrations, offline queue, and reconciliation right is the work. Teams that treat it as a compliance checkbox ship something that transmits most invoices most of the time — and that gap is precisely what a field audit is designed to find.

Start with the prerequisites, insist on sandbox, design the offline path before the happy path, and monitor the queue from day one. If building and maintaining that yourself is not where your business should spend engineering time, an integrated POS gets you the same compliance posture without owning the schema churn.
